practiceSets.passage: At dusk, Kai followed a trail of blue feathers into the empty greenhouse. The glass panes hummed softly, and a silver moth the size of his hand landed on the watering can.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly shows this is an imaginative text?
answers: The invented silver moth and humming glass create an unreal world.
The passage presents a claim with evidence.
The passage lists verified facts about moths.
questions.summary: Invented events and sensory details help create an imaginary world.
questions.hint: Look for details that could not be part of an ordinary factual report.

questions.prompt: What effect does ‘the glass panes hummed softly’ have?
answers: It gives the setting an unusual, almost living quality.
It explains how greenhouse glass is manufactured.
It tells readers to repair the glass.
It proves the greenhouse is unsafe.
questions.summary: The person-like action adds atmosphere and helps the setting feel mysterious.
questions.hint: Ask how the language shapes the mood of the setting.

questions.prompt: Which added sentence would best continue the same imaginative purpose?
answers: Kai whispered, ‘Are you leading me somewhere?’ and the moth lifted into the dark.
Greenhouses are structures used to grow plants.
Please support the school greenhouse fundraiser.
questions.summary: Dialogue and an invented action continue the narrative world.
questions.hint: Choose a continuation that develops characters or events.

questions.prompt: A student says the passage is imaginative only because it contains the word ‘moth’. What is the best correction?
answers: The key evidence is the impossible size, humming glass and mysterious events, not the topic alone.
Any text about an animal is imaginative.
The setting must be real because greenhouses exist.
questions.summary: Text type depends on how features are used, not simply on the topic.
questions.hint: Use specific evidence from the way the writer presents the scene.

practiceSets.passage:
WHY BEES MATTER
Bees move pollen between flowers as they feed. This helps many flowering plants produce seeds and fruit. A labelled diagram beside the paragraph shows pollen on a bee’s body and arrows between two flowers.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of this text?
answers: To explain how bees help flowering plants reproduce
To convince readers to buy honey
To entertain with a bee adventure
To give rules for keeping a pet bee
questions.summary: The text explains a process using facts and a diagram.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is meant to learn.

questions.prompt: Why is the heading ‘WHY BEES MATTER’ useful?
answers: It signals the topic and helps readers locate the section quickly.
It tells readers to agree with every sentence.
questions.summary: Headings organise informative texts and guide readers.
questions.hint: Think about how the heading helps before the paragraph is read.

questions.prompt: What does the labelled diagram add?
answers: It shows the movement of pollen and where it sits on the bee.
It proves bees are the only pollinators.
It changes the text into a story.
It asks readers to plant flowers.
questions.summary: The diagram makes a process and spatial relationship easier to see.
questions.hint: Ask what is easier to understand visually than in words alone.

questions.prompt: How do the paragraph and diagram work together?
answers: The paragraph explains the process while the diagram shows the movement visually.
The paragraph persuades while the diagram entertains.
questions.summary: The two modes complement each other by explaining and showing the same process.
questions.hint: Identify what each mode contributes.

practiceSets.passage: Give our oval more shade. On hot days, the metal seats become uncomfortable by lunchtime. Two shade sails above the seating area would give students a cooler place to rest. Support the proposal at Friday’s student meeting.

questions.prompt: What is the writer mainly trying to do?
answers: Persuade readers to support shade sails
Describe the oval without giving an opinion
questions.summary: The writer states a proposal, gives a reason and asks readers to support it.
questions.hint: Look for a position, reasons and a call to action.

questions.prompt: Which feature most strongly supports the persuasive purpose?
answers: A clear proposal linked to a problem students experience
questions.summary: A claim supported by a relevant reason helps persuade an audience.
questions.hint: Find the feature that gives readers a reason to agree.

questions.prompt: Which words are the clearest call to action?
answers: Support the proposal at Friday’s student meeting.
questions.summary: A call to action directly tells readers what to do next.
questions.hint: Find the words that ask the audience to act.

questions.prompt: Which structure best supports the message?
answers: Problem–solution: hot seats are the problem and shade sails are the proposed solution.
Sequential: steps must be followed in order.
questions.summary: The problem–solution organisation makes the proposal easy to understand.
questions.hint: Identify the problem and the proposed response.

practiceSets.passage: Both rain gauges and weather radar help scientists measure or track rainfall. A rain gauge collects water at one location, while radar can estimate rainfall across a much larger area. Rain gauges provide direct measurements; radar provides wider coverage.

questions.prompt: Which detail is a similarity?
answers: Both help scientists measure or track rainfall.
Only radar collects water in a container.
Rain gauges cover larger areas than radar.
questions.summary: The passage directly states that both tools help with rainfall information.
questions.hint: Look for a feature shared by both subjects.

questions.prompt: Which detail is a difference?
answers: A rain gauge measures one location while radar covers a wider area.
questions.summary: The text contrasts the scale of coverage of the two tools.
questions.hint: Look for the contrast signalled by ‘while’.

questions.prompt: Which text structure is dominant?
questions.summary: The paragraph is organised around similarities and differences between two tools.
questions.hint: Ask how the ideas are related.

questions.prompt: Which word most clearly signals a contrast?
questions.summary: ‘While’ introduces a difference between the two subjects.
questions.hint: Look for a word that separates unlike features.

practiceSets.passage: After three days of heavy rain, water filled the low section of the walking track. The council first placed warning cones there, but the water returned after every storm. Workers later dug a shallow drain beside the track, and the puddle stopped forming.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem?
answers: Water repeatedly flooded the low section of the track.
The council had too many warning cones.
Workers could not find the track.
questions.summary: The recurring puddle is the difficulty the council is trying to address.
questions.hint: Identify what keeps going wrong.

questions.prompt: Why are the warning cones an attempted rather than final solution?
answers: They warned people but did not stop the water returning.
questions.summary: The cones managed safety temporarily but did not fix the cause of the puddle.
questions.hint: Check whether the first action actually removes the problem.

questions.prompt: What was the more effective solution?
answers: Digging a shallow drain beside the track
questions.summary: The drain changed where water flowed, so the puddle stopped forming.
questions.hint: Find the action linked to the successful outcome.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the organisation?
questions.summary: The passage shows a problem, a limited first response and a successful later solution.
questions.hint: Follow how the response to the problem changes.

practiceSets.passage: A row of native shrubs was planted beside the vegetable garden. The shrubs attracted more small insects. Because insect-eating birds followed the insects, the number of caterpillars on the vegetables fell.

questions.prompt: What happened because the shrubs attracted more insects?
questions.summary: The text states that birds followed the increased insects.
questions.hint: Trace what happened next in the chain.

questions.prompt: What was the final effect in the chain?
answers: Fewer caterpillars were found on the vegetables.
questions.summary: The causal chain ends with a fall in caterpillar numbers.
questions.hint: Follow the chain to its last result.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best represents the causal chain?
answers: native shrubs → more insects → more birds → fewer caterpillars
fewer caterpillars → no insects → no shrubs
questions.summary: The passage links each event to the next in that order.
questions.hint: Build the chain using evidence from the paragraph.

questions.prompt: Which structure is dominant?
questions.summary: The ideas are organised around what caused later changes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the paragraph explains reasons and results.

practiceSets.passage: First rinse the reusable jar. Next spoon in two layers of gravel. Then add potting mix and a small fern. Finally mist the soil and place the jar where it gets indirect light.

questions.prompt: Which structure is dominant?
questions.summary: The text gives steps in a particular order.
questions.hint: Look for ordered actions.

questions.prompt: Which words most clearly reveal the structure?
questions.summary: The sequence words show the order of the procedure.
questions.hint: Look for language that tells what comes before and after.

questions.prompt: Why does this structure suit the text’s purpose?
answers: Readers need to know the order in which to complete the steps.
Readers need to compare two jars.
Readers need to decide whether jars are good or bad.
Readers need to imagine a fantasy garden.
questions.summary: Procedures use sequence so readers can carry out actions correctly.
questions.hint: Connect the order to what the reader must do.

questions.prompt: Which change would make the procedure harder to follow?
answers: Removing the order words and mixing the steps
Keeping each step in a separate sentence
questions.summary: Removing order and mixing steps weakens the structure needed for a procedure.
questions.hint: Choose the revision that damages navigation and order.

practiceSets.passage: The spinifex hopping-mouse has large dark eyes, long back feet and a tail longer than its body. Its pale fur blends with sandy ground. It lives in dry inland areas and often shelters in deep burrows during the day.

questions.prompt: Which structure is dominant?
questions.summary: The paragraph groups details about one animal’s appearance and habitat.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text mainly lists characteristics of one topic.

questions.prompt: Which detail describes appearance rather than habitat?
answers: It has large dark eyes and long back feet.
It lives in dry inland areas.
It shelters in burrows during the day.
questions.summary: Eyes and feet describe what the animal looks like.
questions.hint: Separate physical features from where or how it lives.

questions.prompt: Which visual would best complement this paragraph?
answers: A labelled photograph showing the mouse’s long feet, tail and fur colour
A graph of school lunch choices
A poster asking people to vote
questions.summary: A labelled image would add visual detail about the physical features described.
questions.hint: Choose a visual that directly supports the topic.

questions.prompt: Why is this not mainly cause–effect?
answers: Most sentences describe features and habitat rather than explaining a chain of reasons and results.
It has more than one sentence.
Animals cannot appear in cause–effect texts.
questions.summary: Dominant structure depends on how most ideas are organised, not the topic.
questions.hint: Look at what most of the sentences are doing.

practiceSets.passage: A digital article about the Great Barrier Reef has a contents menu, bold key terms, photographs with captions and a map showing reef locations along the Queensland coast.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the contents menu?
answers: To help readers jump to the section they need
To persuade readers to buy a boat
questions.summary: A contents menu helps readers navigate a longer text efficiently.
questions.hint: Think about moving around the article.

questions.prompt: Why might key terms be bold?
answers: To draw attention to important vocabulary
To show the terms are jokes
To indicate they must be skipped
questions.summary: Bold type can highlight vocabulary readers may need to notice or define.
questions.hint: Ask what the formatting makes stand out.

questions.prompt: What does the map contribute?
answers: It shows where reef locations are situated geographically.
It tells a fictional story about a reef.
It proves every reef is the same size.
questions.summary: The map adds spatial information that prose may not show as quickly.
questions.hint: Ask what location information the visual makes clear.

questions.prompt: Why are captions useful beside photographs?
answers: They identify or explain what the reader is seeing.
They turn the article into a persuasive speech.
They make the photographs decorative only.
They replace the need for any facts.
questions.summary: Captions connect an image to specific factual information.
questions.hint: Think about how words help interpret a visual.

practiceSets.passage: Choose a litter-free lunch on Wednesday. Reusable containers can reduce the wrappers left in our bins. Last week, our class filled two whole bins with single-use packaging. A small bar chart shows wrapper counts from Monday to Friday.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s main purpose?
answers: To persuade students to use reusable lunch containers
To explain how plastic is manufactured
To entertain with a lunch story
questions.summary: The text asks readers to take an action and supports it with a reason.
questions.hint: Look for a call to action and supporting evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence provides evidence for the persuasive claim?
answers: Last week, our class filled two whole bins with single-use packaging.
Choose a litter-free lunch on Wednesday.
questions.summary: The two-bin detail is specific evidence showing the size of the waste problem.
questions.hint: Find the measurable information.

questions.prompt: How can the bar chart strengthen the text?
answers: It can show the pattern of wrapper counts as evidence readers can compare.
It replaces the call to action.
It proves reusable containers are free.
questions.summary: A relevant chart can support a persuasive message with visible evidence.
questions.hint: Ask how the visual supports the reason.

questions.prompt: Which combination best explains how the text persuades?
answers: call to action + reason + specific evidence
questions.summary: The text asks readers to act, explains why and supplies evidence.
questions.hint: Identify the features that influence an audience.

practiceSets.passage: The moon jellyfish has a nearly transparent bell with four pale rings visible inside. It drifts through coastal water and uses short tentacles to catch tiny animals. A close-up photograph shows the four rings mentioned in the paragraph.

questions.prompt: What is the text mainly doing?
answers: Giving factual information about a moon jellyfish
questions.summary: The paragraph describes factual characteristics and behaviour.
questions.hint: Ask whether the writer is explaining, persuading or entertaining.

questions.prompt: Which structure is most important?
questions.summary: The text lists characteristics of one subject.
questions.hint: Look at how the details are grouped.

questions.prompt: Why is the close-up photograph useful?
answers: It helps readers see the four rings described in the words.
It asks readers to adopt a jellyfish.
questions.summary: The photograph complements the description by showing a physical feature.
questions.hint: Connect the image to a detail in the words.

questions.prompt: If the photograph did not show four rings, what should a careful reader do?
answers: Notice the mismatch and question whether the image or caption matches the text.
Assume all jellyfish have no rings.
Change the paragraph into a story.
questions.summary: Readers should compare words and visuals and notice when they do not support each other.
questions.hint: Use both modes critically.

practiceSets.passage: The first design for the class bird feeder had a flat roof. Rain soaked the seed, so the class added a sloping cover. After that, rainwater ran off and the seed stayed dry.

questions.prompt: What caused the seed to become wet?
answers: Rain fell onto the feeder with the flat roof.
The class added a sloping cover.
questions.summary: The passage links the flat-roof design and rain with wet seed.
questions.hint: Identify the reason for the unwanted result.

questions.prompt: What solution did the class use?
questions.summary: The sloping cover addressed the problem of rain soaking the seed.
questions.hint: Find the action taken to fix the problem.

questions.prompt: Why could this passage be described using both cause–effect and problem–solution?
answers: It explains why the seed got wet and also how the class fixed the problem.
It only describes colour and size.
questions.summary: A text can contain more than one structure when ideas have more than one relationship.
questions.hint: Look for both a cause/result link and a problem/response link.

questions.prompt: What is the likely purpose of the passage?
answers: To inform readers about how a design was improved
To persuade readers to buy a feeder
To entertain with an imaginary bird
questions.summary: The passage explains a real problem and design change.
questions.hint: Ask what readers are meant to understand from the events.

testSets.passage: The council wants more families to use the new bike path. A leaflet says, ‘Try the river route this weekend—six kilometres of separated path with rest stops along the way.’ A simple map marks the route and rest stops.

questions.prompt: What is the leaflet mainly trying to do?
answers: Persuade families to try the bike path
Describe a river without a viewpoint
questions.summary: The leaflet uses an invitation plus benefits to encourage action.
questions.hint: Identify what the audience is being encouraged to do.

questions.prompt: How does the map support the purpose?
answers: It helps families visualise the route and practical rest-stop locations.
It proves everyone will enjoy cycling.
questions.summary: The map adds useful spatial information that makes the proposed action easier to understand.
questions.hint: Ask what practical information the visual adds.

questions.prompt: Which feature is strongest evidence of persuasion?
questions.summary: The imperative directly invites the audience to act.
questions.hint: Find the clearest call to action.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains how the leaflet’s features work together?
answers: Invitation, route details and map make the suggestion both appealing and usable.
The map makes the text imaginative.
The route details form a recipe.
questions.summary: Words persuade while practical details and a map support the reader’s decision.
questions.hint: Combine purpose with the function of the visual.

testSets.passage: During a heatwave, the school garden wilted over weekends. Extra watering on Friday did not last. The class installed a slow-drip container beside each plant, and the soil remained damp until Monday.

questions.prompt: What was the problem?
questions.summary: The repeated drying is the issue the class needed to solve.
questions.hint: Identify the difficulty before the response.

questions.prompt: Why was extra Friday watering not the final solution?
answers: It did not keep the soil damp for the whole weekend.
It made the plants grow too quickly.
questions.summary: The first attempt did not fully solve the problem.
questions.hint: Check the outcome of the first response.

questions.prompt: Which action solved the problem more effectively?
questions.summary: The slow-drip system kept moisture available longer.
questions.hint: Find the response linked to the successful result.

questions.prompt: Which structure best describes the paragraph?
questions.summary: The paragraph centres on a problem and changing attempts to solve it.
questions.hint: Track the problem and responses.

testSets.passage: A facts page about echidnas includes the heading ‘Finding food’, a photograph with a caption, and this sentence: ‘Echidnas use strong claws to break into ant nests, then collect ants with a long sticky tongue.’

questions.prompt: What does the heading help the reader do?
answers: Locate information about how echidnas get food
Decide whether echidnas are good pets
questions.summary: The heading identifies the topic of the section.
questions.hint: Think about finding specific information quickly.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a caption under the photograph?
answers: Identify or explain something shown in the image
Turn the page into a story
questions.summary: Captions help readers interpret images in relation to the text.
questions.hint: Ask what words beneath an image usually clarify.

questions.prompt: Which word in the sentence most clearly shows order?
questions.summary: ‘Then’ shows that one action follows another.
questions.hint: Look for a word showing what happens next.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why these features suit an informative text?
answers: The heading organises information, the caption clarifies the image, and the sentence explains behaviour.
They ask the reader to vote.
They make the text a poem.
questions.summary: Each feature helps readers locate, interpret or understand factual information.
questions.hint: Explain how the features help the reader learn.

testSets.passage: Both electric buses and diesel buses can carry many passengers. Electric buses run on batteries and produce no exhaust at the vehicle. Diesel buses use fuel and release exhaust while operating. A table lists each bus type, energy source and local exhaust.

questions.prompt: Which detail is a similarity?
answers: Both release exhaust at the vehicle.
questions.summary: The passage states a feature shared by both bus types.
questions.hint: Find what applies to each subject.

questions.prompt: Which detail is a difference?
answers: Electric buses use batteries while diesel buses use fuel.
questions.summary: The energy source differs between the two bus types.
questions.hint: Look for contrasting details.

questions.prompt: Why is the table useful?
answers: It lets readers compare the same features across both bus types quickly.
It turns the text into a story.
It proves one bus is always better.
questions.summary: Tables can organise comparable information into aligned categories.
questions.hint: Ask what is easier to compare in rows or columns.

questions.prompt: Which structure is dominant?
questions.summary: The paragraph and table are organised around similarities and differences.
questions.hint: Identify the main relationship between ideas.
